description: Same as the paper-traded baseline (12-1 lookback, 20 equal-weighted stocks, cash when NIFTY 50 is below its 200-day average), with one change: stocks are ranked on 12-1 return divided by annualised volatility instead of raw return.
hypothesis: Raw momentum rankings favour high-volatility stocks whose past return is partly noise and which drive momentum crashes (Barroso & Santa-Clara; Daniel & Moskowitz). Ranking on return per unit of volatility picks steadier trends, the same normalisation NSE uses for Nifty200 Momentum 30. It should cut drawdowns and turnover and raise return per rupee at risk. Only one knob changes, so any lead over the baseline is less likely to be fitted noise.
lessons: On NIFTY 200, raw 12-1 strength is the main source of the edge. Penalising volatility at the ranking stage removes the high-momentum winners that drive the big years. A 3-point smaller drawdown does not pay for a 2.4% a year return drag. If volatility is used at all, it should control risk, through position size, and not decide which stocks get picked.
title: Volatility-adjusted 12-1 momentum, 20 stocks, NIFTY 200-day filter

training.why_not: no better than the momentum rule already paper-traded (-2.37% a year against it)

change_note: Ranking goes back to raw 12-1 return, the same as the baseline, and volatility now sets sizing only (inverse_volatility). This keeps the stock selection and aims to cut drawdown. The 60-day window and 2x cap cannot be set in this format, so the engine defaults apply.
description: Same selection as the baseline: the top 20 NIFTY 200 stocks by 12-1 return, cash when NIFTY 50 is below its 200-day average. Only the sizing changes, to inverse volatility. The format has no keys for the 60-day window or the 2x cap, so those come from the engine's inverse_volatility defaults and may differ from the request.
hypothesis: Version 1 lost return because ranking by return over volatility swapped strong winners for calmer, weaker names. Keeping the raw 12-1 ranking keeps those winners. Sizing by inverse volatility should give less weight to the stocks most prone to crashes (the momentum crash effect) and trim drawdowns without changing which stocks are held. Expect a worst fall below 23% with a return close to the baseline. A t of 2 or more over the baseline is unlikely, because the holdings are identical and only the weights differ.
lessons: Within a 20-stock momentum basket, volatility is part of the return source, so down-weighting it gives up return for only a slight cut in drawdown. Weighting tweaks inside the same selection move results by a couple of percent and tend to cost more than they save. A bigger difference is more likely to come from what is selected or from when the strategy goes to cash than from how positions are sized. The baseline remains the version to beat.
title: Raw 12-1 momentum, top 20, inverse-volatility sizing, NIFTY 200-day filter

training.why_not: no better than the momentum rule already paper-traded (-2.28% a year against it)

change_note: Back to the baseline's raw 12-1 score and equal weights, since volatility-scaling lost return twice. Concentrated from 20 to 12 stocks to capture the stronger top-rank premium, with an own-200-day trend check per stock to keep crash-prone names out.
description: Rank NIFTY 200 on 12-1 momentum and hold the top 12 equally weighted, but only stocks still closing above their own 200-session average. Hold cash while NIFTY 50 is below its 200-day average. Monthly rebalance. The only changes from the baseline are concentration and a per-stock trend check.
hypothesis: Both volatility-scaling attempts cut drawdown but also cut return, so risk-dampening is the wrong direction for beating the baseline. The momentum premium is strongest in the top ranks: the spread between the top and next deciles is well documented, so holding 12 instead of 20 should raise return. Concentration adds stock-specific crash risk. Requiring each stock to be above its own 200-session average drops names whose long-run winner status is already rolling over, which is the main source of momentum crashes. That should keep the worst fall under 30%.
lessons: Fewer stocks is mostly a variance dial on the same signal. It adds return in a few trend years and does not improve consistency or drawdown. Testing more position counts (10, 15) would be searching for a lucky parameter and undermines the pre-registered test. The paper-traded 20-stock baseline stays the rule, and later ideas should add independent information rather than retune holdings count.
title: Concentrated 12-1 momentum, 12 stocks, own-trend confirmation

training.why_not: its lead over the paper-traded rule could be luck: t = 1.65 (needs 2)

change_note: Added a 50-session own-trend filter to the baseline. It is a selection change that brings recent-trend information the 12-1 score ignores. Holdings count, weighting and ranking are left alone, per earlier lessons.
description: Paper-traded baseline (12-1 raw momentum, top 20, equal weight, cash when NIFTY 50 is below its 200-day average). One change: a stock is eligible only if it closes above its own 50-session average. The ranking, holdings count, sizing and market filter are unchanged.
hypothesis: 12-1 momentum skips the latest month, so it keeps buying stocks whose trend has already broken. Those are where momentum crashes start. A 200-day own-trend filter adds little, because a top-decile 12-month winner is almost always above its 200-day average. A 50-day filter adds independent, recent information: it drops names already rolling over and passes the slot to the next-ranked stock in an intact trend. If this works, the lead should come from fewer losses in choppy years (2011, 2013, 2018, 2019, 2022), not from a few trend years. Risk: it may clash with short-term reversal and add turnover, so a t below 2 is a likely result.
lessons: A per-stock short-trend filter on top of 12-1 momentum is mostly redundant, because top-momentum stocks are already above their trends. Its main effect is extra turnover and early exits in trending markets. Making the filter slower would mostly bring the result back to the baseline rather than beat it. Any real improvement probably has to come from a different dimension, such as ranking quality, volatility-adjusted momentum, or position sizing, not from more exit filters.
title: 12-1 momentum, 20 stocks, 50-day own-trend confirmation, NIFTY 200-day filter

training.why_not: no better than the momentum rule already paper-traded (-0.57% a year against it)

change_note: Dropped the 50-day own-trend filter, which added nothing (-0.57%/yr). Added a loose 50% volatility cap to exclude only crash-prone extreme names, while keeping raw-return ranking, which earlier tests showed is the edge.
description: Same paper-traded rule: rank NIFTY 200 on 12-1 return, hold top 20 equal-weight, cash when NIFTY 50 is below its 200-day average. One change: stocks with annualised volatility above 50% are not eligible. Ranking stays raw return, so this only removes the extreme tail, not ordinary high-volatility winners.
hypothesis: Momentum crashes (Daniel-Moskowitz) concentrate in the highest-volatility, lottery-like losers-turned-winners, often junk rebounds after selloffs. Earlier tests showed that penalising volatility across the whole ranking cuts the winners that drive returns. A loose cap instead removes only the extreme tail, which tends to give back gains in reversals. Expect similar trend-year returns with fewer sharp single-name losses. This is one knob set from theory, not a sweep. A t>=2 lead is unlikely, so read a fail as evidence that the baseline is robust.
lessons: In this universe, momentum's edge comes from the high-volatility, crash-prone names, so filtering on crash risk cuts the right tail without trimming the left tail. Drawdown is already set by the market-level 200-day filter, so stock-level risk screens don't move worst fall. Future ideas should either add return (better ranking or timing) or attack drawdown at the portfolio or regime level, not exclude stocks.
title: 12-1 momentum, 20 stocks, exclude crash-prone names (vol cap 50%), NIFTY 200d

training.why_not: no better than the momentum rule already paper-traded (-5.32% a year against it)

change_note: Lookback cut from 12 to 6 months, nothing else changed: tests whether a faster formation window, as used in NSE's own momentum index, catches leadership changes earlier.
description: Rank NIFTY 200 stocks on their 6-month return, skipping the latest month. Hold the top 20 equally weighted and rebalance monthly. Hold cash while NIFTY 50 is below its 200-session average. Only the lookback differs from the paper-traded baseline.
hypothesis: NSE's own momentum index blends 6- and 12-month returns, and emerging-market momentum tends to be shorter-lived than US momentum. A 6-1 window should pick up new leadership after regime shifts such as 2009, 2014, 2020 and 2023 sooner. It should also drop fading 12-month winners earlier. Earlier tests showed volatility screens and weighting only remove return, so this changes what is selected, not how it is filtered or sized. Expect higher yearly return than 12-1 at similar drawdown under the same market filter. Risk: more turnover at 0.2%.
lessons: A shorter lookback adds turnover and cost without adding edge. Its wins cluster in sharp-recovery years, which looks like timing luck. The 12-1 signal with the 200-day filter is hard to beat by retuning the lookback. Cutting costs and turnover, or adding an independent signal, is more promising than changing the horizon.
title: 6-1 momentum, 20 stocks, NIFTY 200-day filter (shorter formation)

training.why_not: no better than the momentum rule already paper-traded (-1.25% a year against it)

change_note: Market filter shortened from 200 to 100 sessions; selection and sizing left as in the paper rule. Earlier lessons say gains are more likely to come from when the strategy goes to cash than from re-weighting or re-ranking.
description: Same selection as the paper rule: 12-1 return, top 20, equal weight. The only change is the market filter. It holds cash while NIFTY 50 is below its 100-session average instead of its 200-session average. This tests the timing of going to cash, the one lever earlier days flagged but never tried.
hypothesis: Momentum losses cluster in sharp market reversals: fast sell-offs (2011, 2018, Feb-Mar 2020) and V-shaped rebounds (2009, mid-2020). The 200-day average reacts late on both sides, so the basket takes much of the fall and then sits in cash through the early recovery. A 100-day trend is still a standard trend signal but turns about twice as fast. It should exit earlier and re-enter sooner, lifting return over the baseline without adding a selection knob. The cost is more switches at 0.2% each and more false exits in choppy years. Prior odds of reaching t >= 2 on one timing change are modest.
lessons: Making the market-trend filter faster just trades V-recovery gains for whipsaw losses in trending years, so the net is about zero. The baseline's 200-day filter is not the bottleneck. Small drawdown improvements of 1-2 points are within noise and do not justify replacing a rule already being paper-traded. With one version left, tweaking filter speed again is unlikely to produce a significant lead.
title: 12-1 momentum, 20 stocks, faster NIFTY 100-day cash filter

training.why_not: no better than the momentum rule already paper-traded (-0.57% a year against it)

change_note: skip_months 1 -> 0: tests whether the US-derived short-term-reversal skip is needed on NSE large caps (NSE's momentum indexes don't skip); everything else is identical to the baseline.
description: Same as the paper-traded rule (12-month return rank, top 20, equal weight, cash when NIFTY 50 is below its 200-day average), except the most recent month is kept in the ranking instead of skipped. It is a one-knob change, in line with how NSE's own momentum indexes rank without a skip month.
hypothesis: The 1-month skip exists because of short-term reversal in US small caps. In liquid Indian large caps, reversal is weak and recent strength tends to continue, as NSE's no-skip momentum index suggests. Keeping the latest month should rank fresh leaders sooner and drop fading names earlier, adding return without more drawdown. Expect a small lead; a t below 1.65 means the skip month should stay.
lessons: Removing the skip month gives a modest, regime-dependent gain, concentrated in trending markets and recent years, not a uniform improvement. Judge future changes on years beating the baseline and luck_t vs baseline, not on CAGR. Keep 12-0 as a candidate, but it needs a change that makes the gain more consistent across years before calling it better.
title: 12-0 momentum, 20 stocks, NIFTY 200-day filter (no skip month)

change_note: Ranking changed from raw 12-0 return to 12-0 return divided by 12-month annualised volatility, everything else unchanged. Aim: a steadier lead and fewer extreme down days. Prior 12-1 evidence warns this may cost return.
description: Same as the passing 12-0 version (12-month return with no skip month, 20 stocks, equal weight, cash when NIFTY 50 is below its 200-day average). The only change is that stocks are ranked on 12-month return divided by annualised daily volatility over the same window.
hypothesis: Ranking on return per unit of volatility should favour smoother trends. These are less prone to momentum crashes and gap-downs, so the lead over the 12-1 baseline could be steadier year to year and the -12.9% worst day smaller. Risk: the 12-1 version of this ranking lost 2.37%/yr because it dropped the high-volatility winners. A pass needs the no-skip signal to keep enough raw strength to stay ahead with t >= 1.65. Otherwise, volatility belongs in risk control, not selection.
lessons: Change one variable per version, because v2 mixed a ranking change with a lookback change and the result cannot be attributed. Risk-adjusting the ranking seems to buy small drawdown gains at the cost of upside in strong trending years. Check recent-year consistency against the baseline, not only the full-period average.
title: Risk-adjusted 12-0 momentum, 20 stocks, NIFTY 200-day filter

training.why_not: no better than the momentum rule already paper-traded (-1.31% a year against it)

change_note: Restored skip_months to 1 and kept the return/volatility score, to isolate risk adjustment. Warning: this duplicates M-20261020 vol-adjusted 12-1 v1 (-2.37%/yr, t -1.6). It is likely a wasted slot; 12-0 raw momentum (version 1, passed) is the stronger lead.
description: Ranks NIFTY 200 stocks by 12-1 return divided by annualised volatility, skipping the most recent month. Holds the top 20 at equal weight and rebalances monthly. Goes to cash while NIFTY 50 is below its 200-session average. Only the score changes from the baseline.
hypothesis: Return-per-unit-risk may pick steadier trends than raw return, which could cut reversals and turnover. Restoring the skip month isolates the effect of risk adjustment alone. Caveat: this exact configuration already ran on 2026-10-20 (M-20261020-volatility-adjusted-12-1-momentum-20-sto-v1) and lost 2.37%/yr against the baseline (t -1.6). Expect the same failure. This run only confirms that risk adjustment adds nothing.
lessons: Vol-adjusting 12-1 momentum on NSE gives up return for only small drawdown gains. It also lost every year since 2016, which suggests the old edge has faded. The baseline's 200-day filter already supplies most of the downside protection, so further risk scaling of the ranking adds little. Three versions of this idea have not beaten the baseline; drop it.
title: Risk-adjusted 12-1 momentum, 20 stocks, NIFTY 200-day filter

training.why_not: no better than the momentum rule already paper-traded (-2.39% a year against it)

change_note: Keeps v1's 12-0 raw momentum (the only passing version) and adds one slow 200-day own-trend gate to drop broken former winners. Selection, sizing and market filter are otherwise unchanged, so any difference can be attributed to the gate.
description: Builds on today's passing v1 (12-0 momentum). Ranks NIFTY 200 stocks on their full 12-month return with no skip month, holds the top 20 equally, and keeps only names closing above their own 200-session average. Holds cash while NIFTY 50 is below its 200-day average.
hypothesis: In NSE large caps, short-term reversal is weak, so skipping the last month throws away signal (v1: +2.85%/yr, t 2.06). A slow stock-level 200-day trend gate should drop names whose 12-month gain came early and has since rolled over, which is a known source of momentum crashes, without the turnover of the 50-day gate that failed. It is expected to bind rarely, so the effect may be small. Caution: about 10 versions have been tried, so v1's t of 2.06 is itself marginal. If this does not clearly pass, prefer v1 or the baseline over more tuning.
lessons: A stock-level trend filter on top of 12-1 momentum and the NIFTY filter gives a small, uneven edge. It comes from a few trending years, not a steady improvement. Using the last version today to tune the filter length or add a buffer would mostly fit noise. The baseline stays the honest default. v4 is a candidate worth re-testing on out-of-sample or paper-trading data, but it is not a proven upgrade. Higher costs and a worse worst day should be watched.
title: 12-0 momentum, 20 stocks, own 200-day trend gate, NIFTY 200-day filter

change_note: Market filter 200 to 300 sessions, everything else equal to baseline; tests the untested slower side of filter speed (the faster 100-day side failed) to cut whipsaw turnover in choppy years.
description: The baseline paper rule with one change: hold cash only while NIFTY 50 is below its 300-session average instead of its 200-session average. Ranking, skip month, holdings, equal weighting and costs are unchanged, so any difference comes from the regime filter alone.
hypothesis: The baseline spends 25% of months in cash, and its weakest years (2011, 2013, 2015-16, 2018-19) were choppy markets where NIFTY kept crossing its 200-day average. That suggests whipsaw costs: selling near lows, rebuying higher, and paying 0.2% each way. A faster 100-day filter made this worse, so a slower filter should flip less often and miss fewer momentum rebounds. Risk: it exits later in fast crashes like 2020, which could deepen the worst fall. If it fails, filter speed is settled in both directions.
lessons: Tuning the market-filter length is a weak lever: it shifts when we are in cash, not which stocks we hold, and trades drawdown for noisy gains. Small lookback tweaks like 200 vs 300 days risk overfitting and will not clear t >= 1.65 against the baseline. Expect a real edge from the stock-selection side, not from filter timing.
title: 12-1 momentum, 20 stocks, slower NIFTY 300-day cash filter

training.why_not: its lead over the paper-traded rule could be luck: t = 1.01 (needs 1.65)

change_note: v1's slower 300-day market filter was not significant (t 1.01), so it goes back to 200. This version adds only a per-stock 200-day trend gate to the baseline, to measure the gate's own effect separately from the 12-0 lookback change it was bundled with in the earlier pass.
description: The paper-traded baseline (12-1 momentum, top 20, equal weight, cash when NIFTY 50 is below its 200-day average), with one change: a stock is only eligible if it closes above its own 200-session average. Holdings, lookback, skip month and market filter all match the baseline, so any difference comes from the gate.
hypothesis: Trend confirmation: a top 12-1 stock already trading below its own 200-day average is often a stale winner rolling over, and such names drive momentum crashes. The slow 200-day gate drops only those names. It keeps the high-volatility leaders that drive the edge, unlike vol caps or the 50-day filter, which caused churn. The earlier pass mixed this gate with 12-0, so this test separates out the gate's own effect. Expect a small lead with lower turnover drag than the 50-day test, and worst fall at or below baseline.
lessons: Trend filters on single stocks mostly duplicate what 12-1 momentum and the market-level 200-day filter already do, so they are not a source of independent edge here. Changes to filters on the same ranking are unlikely to reach t > 1.65 against this baseline. To get a separable edge, change how stocks are ranked (risk-adjusted or residual momentum) instead of adding more trend gates.
title: 12-1 momentum, 20 stocks, own 200-day trend gate, NIFTY 200-day filter

training.why_not: its lead over the paper-traded rule could be luck: t = 0.44 (needs 1.65)

change_note: Combines 12-0 (no skip month; passed, t 2.06) with today's slower 300-day NIFTY filter (+2.3%/yr, t 1.01). Both values come from earlier single-change tests, so no new knob is added. Ranking and timing are separate parts of the rule, so their gains should add.
description: Rank NIFTY 200 stocks on the last 12 months' return with no skip month. Hold the top 20 equal-weighted and rebalance monthly. Hold cash while NIFTY 50 is below its 300-session average. This combines two changes that were each tested alone, with no new parameter values.
hypothesis: Each change was already tested by itself on this data. 12-0 gave +2.85%/yr over the baseline (t 2.06): recent strength carries on in Indian large caps rather than reversing. The 300-day filter gave +2.30%/yr (t 1.01) by cutting whipsaw cash exits in trending years. They act on different things, ranking versus timing, so their gains should add up. Risk: worst fall nears 29%, still under 35%. Caveat: the 300-day value was chosen after seeing that result, so this is a weaker test than a fresh idea.
lessons: The slower trend filter trades drawdown protection for exposure. The CAGR lead roughly matches the extra time invested, and the worse drawdown fits that. Change one element at a time to separate the effect of the momentum signal (12-0 vs 12-1) and universe from the effect of the filter speed. The recent 2025 underperformance against both baseline and benchmark is a warning sign.
title: 12-0 momentum, 20 stocks, slower NIFTY 300-day cash filter

change_note: Market filter goes back from 300 to 200 days, so only 12-0 differs from the baseline. This repeats M-20261110 12-0 v1 (+2.85%/yr, t 2.06) as a deliberate check that splits v3's lead into its signal part and its slower-filter part.
description: Rank NIFTY 200 stocks on 12-0 return, hold the top 20 equal-weight, rebalance monthly, and hold cash while NIFTY 50 is below its 200-day average. This is the paper-traded baseline with only the skip month removed. Note: there is no NIFTY 300 universe here; the 300 was the length of the cash filter.
hypothesis: If v3's +5.12%/yr lead came mostly from the slower 300-day filter, then restoring the 200-day filter should drop the lead toward the +2.85%/yr (t 2.06) that 12-0 alone showed earlier. Worst fall should return to about 22%. Most of the lead staying would mean the signal, not the extra exposure, drives it. A lead smaller than about +2.85% would suggest the extra market exposure, and its 29.7% worst fall, was paying for v3's gain.
lessons: The variant mainly amplifies strong trending years and gives back some ground in choppy or reversal years such as 2020-21. A 2.8% lead with 53% of years ahead and t near 2, after several tries, should be treated as possibly noise rather than a proven edge. Using the single remaining version to tune further would raise overfitting risk more than it would add information. If v4 is adopted, paper-trade it alongside the baseline and expect returns close to the baseline's.
title: 12-0 momentum, 20 stocks, NIFTY 200-day filter (isolation re-test)

change_note: Kept 12-0 (passed twice, t about 2.05) and widened from 20 to 30 holdings. This tests whether the edge holds across the ranking or is concentration luck; no other knob was changed.
description: Ranks NIFTY 200 stocks on their full 12-month return with no skip month and holds the top 30 equally weighted. Goes to cash while NIFTY 50 is below its 200-session average. It keeps the only signal change that has passed so far (12-0) and asks whether that edge is broad across the ranking or rests on a few top names.
hypothesis: If dropping the skip month adds real information, a 30-stock basket should keep most of the roughly 2.8%/yr lead over the baseline, with steadier year-by-year excess and a t near or above 1.65. If the lead shrinks to noise, the earlier 12-0 passes most likely came from a handful of concentrated trend-year winners, and 12-1 with 20 stocks remains the honest rule. This is a pre-registered check on breadth, not a hunt for a better holdings count.
lessons: Holding count is not where the edge lies. More names give marginally lower drawdown but cost about 1.6% a year, and the hit is largest in the best momentum years. Going the other way (fewer names) is mostly a hindsight-prone concentration bet. Further tuning of position count is unlikely to beat the paper-traded baseline. A real improvement needs a different signal or risk rule, not a different breadth of the same signal.
title: 12-0 momentum, 30 stocks, NIFTY 200-day filter (breadth robustness test)

training.why_not: no better than the momentum rule already paper-traded (-1.58% a year against it)

change_note: Holdings changed from 30 to 25, with 12-0 ranking and the NIFTY 200 filter unchanged. This checks whether the 12-0 edge fades smoothly with breadth (real but concentrated) or breaks between 20 and 30 (fragile). It is a robustness check, not tuning toward a pass.
description: Rank NIFTY 200 stocks on their full 12-month return with no skip month. Hold the top 25, equal-weighted, and rebalance monthly. Hold cash while NIFTY 50 is below its 200-session average. This is the 12-0 candidate with breadth set halfway between the passing 20-stock version and today's failing 30-stock version.
hypothesis: 12-0 with 20 stocks passed twice (+2.8%/yr, t about 2.05), but today's 30-stock version lost 1.6%/yr. If the 12-0 edge is real and sits in the top ranks, widening from 20 to 30 should dilute it smoothly, so 25 stocks should land in between (roughly +0.5 to +1.5%/yr) with similar drawdown. If 25 lands far outside that range, the 12-0 result is fragile to breadth and should not replace the paper rule. This is a robustness test chosen in advance, not a search for the best holdings count. I expect it to fail the t >= 1.65 bar.
lessons: Portfolio size between 20 and 25 is a flat parameter: return and drawdown are essentially unchanged, so it is not a lever for beating the baseline. Small tweaks to breadth of the same 12-1 ranking mostly reshuffle the marginal names and produce year-to-year noise, not an edge. To get t > 1.65 versus the baseline, the change needs to alter which stocks get picked or when the strategy is exposed, not just how many.
title: 12-0 momentum, 25 stocks, NIFTY 200-day filter (breadth monotonicity check)

training.why_not: its lead over the paper-traded rule could be luck: t = 0.36 (needs 1.65)

change_note: Holdings cut from 25 (v2) to 15, everything else unchanged. This finishes the monotonicity check of 12-0 momentum across breadth, to tell a real top-rank edge from a lucky 20-stock result. It is not a search for the best count.
description: Rank NIFTY 200 stocks by 12-month return with no skip month and hold the top 15, equal weighted. Rebalance monthly. Hold cash while NIFTY 50 is below its 200-session average. This completes today's pre-registered breadth sweep of the 12-0 signal (30, 25, 20, now 15). It is a diagnostic, not a new tuning knob.
hypothesis: If 12-0's lead comes from real strength in the top ranks, the lead over the paper rule should grow as holdings shrink. So far it does: -1.58%/yr at 30, +0.68% at 25, +2.8% at 20. At 15 it should be at least +2.8%/yr, with t >= 1.65 and worst fall under 35%. If the lead falls back or t drops, the 20-stock pass was a lucky point, and the 12-0 idea should be dropped in favour of the baseline. Pre-registered: no further holdings counts will be tested either way.
lessons: Fewer names amplify momentum in strong trend years at the price of worse single-day tails. The 200-day filter drives drawdown control regardless of how many names are held. Change one thing at a time so the gain can be attributed. Treat a lead that rests on two or three standout years with suspicion until isolated.
title: 12-0 momentum, 15 stocks, NIFTY 200-day filter (breadth monotonicity, tight end)

change_note: Restored skip_months to 1 (12-1) and kept 15 holdings, so the only difference from the baseline is concentration. This isolates whether v3's lead came from holding fewer stocks or from the 12-0 lookback.
description: Same as the paper-traded baseline (12-1 momentum, equal weight, NIFTY 200-day cash filter) except it holds 15 stocks instead of 20. This changes one variable against the baseline so we can tell whether v3's lead came from concentration or from dropping the skip month.
hypothesis: If concentration from 20 to 15 names is the real source of v3's +4.3%/yr lead, this version should keep most of that lead (t >= 1.65) with drawdown near 23%. If the lead collapses, the 12-0 lookback was the driver. Caveat: 12-0 has already passed several times today and on earlier days, and v1/v2 showed lead rising as holdings fell. Holdings count has now been searched (12, 15, 20, 25, 30), so any pass here also carries multiple-testing risk and should be confirmed in paper trading, not adopted on backtest alone.
lessons: Changing how many stocks the rule holds mostly trades risk for return. It cannot produce a lead over the baseline that passes the luck test. Gains that sit in two or three momentum boom years should not be trusted. Future ideas should change the signal or the risk control, for example weighting by volatility or a different lookback, and still beat the baseline in more than half the years. The hindsight bias in the absolute numbers also argues against chasing small CAGR gains.
title: 12-1 momentum, 15 stocks, NIFTY 200-day filter (driver isolation)

training.why_not: its lead over the paper-traded rule could be luck: t = 1.43 (needs 1.65)
